title: Easy exam 4
about: Ten single-choice questions on the basics: one concept each, with the classic look-alike options.

questions.title: Find regular files by name
questions.text: Which command lists the regular files whose name ends in `.conf` under `/etc`?

options.t: `find -name "*.conf" /etc`
options.why: The starting directory must come before the tests: `find` complains "paths must precede expression".

options.t: `find /etc -type d -name "*.conf"`
options.why: `-type d` selects directories, not regular files.

options.t: `find /etc -type f -name "*.conf"`
options.why: `-type f` keeps regular files and the quoted pattern is matched by `find` itself.

options.t: `find /etc -f -name "*.conf"`
options.why: `-f` is not a test of `find`; the type of file is selected with `-type`.

questions.title: Numeric order
questions.text: The file `nums` contains the lines `9`, `10` and `100`. Which command prints them in the order `9`, `10`, `100`?

options.t: `sort nums`
options.why: Alphabetical order compares character by character: `10`, `100`, `9`.

options.t: `sort -n nums`
options.why: `-n` compares the lines as numbers.

options.t: `sort -r nums`
options.why: `-r` reverses the alphabetical order: `9`, `100`, `10`.

options.t: `sort -u nums`
options.why: `-u` removes duplicate lines but the order stays alphabetical: `10`, `100`, `9`.

options.t: It gives write permission to the group and to the others.
options.why: `-` removes permissions; `+` would add them.

options.t: It removes write permission from the owner and from the group.
options.why: `g` and `o` are group and others; the owner is `u`.

options.t: It removes write permission from the group and from the others.
options.why: `go` selects those two classes, `-` removes and `w` is the write permission.

options.t: It sets the permissions of the group and the others to exactly write only.
options.why: Setting an exact value would use `=`.

questions.title: Job control
questions.text: You started `sort bigfile` and suspended it with Ctrl+Z; `jobs` shows it as job number 1. Which statement is TRUE?

options.t: `fg` suspends the job again if it is running in the background.
options.why: `fg` brings a job to the foreground; it never suspends it.

options.t: The job number 1 is the PID of the process.
options.why: The job number is a counter of the current shell, the PID is assigned by the system.

options.t: `bg %1` resumes it and leaves it running in the background.
options.why: `bg` resumes a suspended job without waiting for it.

options.t: `jobs` lists all the processes of all the users of the system.
options.why: `jobs` shows only the jobs of the current shell session.

questions.title: Commands that ignore stdin
questions.text: Which statement about input redirection with `<` is FALSE?

options.t: `wc -l < names.txt` prints only the number of lines, without the file name.
options.why: True: `wc` reads stdin and does not know a file name.

options.t: `sort < names.txt` gives the same lines as `sort names.txt`.
options.why: True: both read the file, one through stdin and the other by name.

options.t: `ls < docs` lists the contents of the directory `docs`.
options.why: False: `ls` does not read stdin, so it lists the current directory and `docs` is ignored.

options.t: `cat < names.txt` shows the file because `cat` reads stdin when it gets no file name.
options.why: True: with no arguments `cat` reads its standard input.

options.t: `rm notes` on a directory called `notes` fails with "Is a directory".
options.why: True: directories need `-r`.

options.t: `rm -r project` deletes the directory `project` and everything inside it.
options.why: True: `-r` is recursive.

options.t: `rm -f report.txt` asks for confirmation before deleting.
options.why: False: `-f` forces the deletion without asking; the option that asks is `-i`.

options.t: `rm -i report.txt` asks before deleting the file.
options.why: True: `-i` is interactive, useful for root.

questions.title: A sudoers line
questions.text: `/etc/sudoers` contains the line `%staff ALL=(ALL) ALL`. Which statement is TRUE?

options.t: It defines a user whose name is `%staff`.
options.why: The `%` marks a group name, not a user.

options.t: Every member of the group `staff` may run any command as any user.
options.why: The `%` prefix selects a group; `ALL` in each field means any host, any target user and any command.

options.t: Only the user `root` may use `sudo`, and `staff` is the machine name.
options.why: The first field is who may use `sudo`; here it is a group, not a machine.

options.t: Members of `staff` become root only after typing the password of root.
options.why: `sudo` asks for the password of the user who runs it; knowing root's password is not needed.

questions.title: grep counting
questions.text: `animals` has four lines: `cat`, `Dog`, `dog food` and `bird`. What does `grep -ci dog animals` print?

options.why: That is the result without `-i`: only `dog food` has a lower case `dog`.
`-i` ignores case, so `Dog` and `dog food` match, and `-c` prints how many lines matched.
That would be the lines that do not contain `dog` with `grep -vc`, which is a different option.
That is the total number of lines in the file, not the number that match.

questions.title: Name, count and first argument
questions.text: `show.sh` has execute permission and contains `echo "$0 has $# args, first is $1"`. What does `./show.sh red green` print?

options.t: `show.sh has 2 args, first is red`
options.why: `$0` is the name used to call the script, so it includes the `./`.

options.t: `./show.sh has 3 args, first is ./show.sh`
options.why: `$#` does not count `$0`, and `$1` is the first argument, not the script.

options.t: `./show.sh has 2 args, first is red`
options.why: `$0` is the command as typed, `$#` counts the two arguments and `$1` is the first.

options.t: `./show.sh has 2 args, first is green`
options.why: Arguments are numbered from the left: `$1` is `red`.

questions.title: Exported and plain variables
questions.text: You run `COLOR=blue` and then `export SIZE=big`. What does `bash -c 'echo "[$COLOR] [$SIZE]"'` print?

options.t: `[blue] [big]`
options.why: Only exported variables reach the new process; `COLOR` was not exported.

options.t: `[blue] []`
options.why: It is the other way round: `SIZE` was exported and `COLOR` was not.
`bash -c` starts a child process, which inherits `SIZE` but not `COLOR`.
`export` exists precisely to pass a variable on to the child processes.
